'''Journal Square''' is a business district, residential area, and transportation hub in [[Jersey City, New Jersey]]. It is named for the newspaper ''[[Jersey Journal]]'', whose headquarters were located there from 1911 to 2013.<ref name = sale>{{cite news   | last = Rose Sibayan   | first = Reena   | title = Jersey Journal to move headquarters to Secaucus in the fall   | newspaper = The Jersey Journal   | date = August 15, 2013   | url = http://www.nj.com/hudson/index.ssf/2013/08/jersey_journal_to_move_headquarters_to_secaucus_in_the_fall.html   | access-date = July 30, 2014   | archive-date = January 7, 2014   | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140107201900/http://www.nj.com/hudson/index.ssf/2013/08/jersey_journal_to_move_headquarters_to_secaucus_in_the_fall.html   | url-status = live }}</ref> The "square" itself is at the intersection of [[County Route 501 (New Jersey)|Kennedy Boulevard]] and [[Bergen-Lafayette, Jersey City|Bergen Avenue]]. The broader area extends to and includes [[Bergen Square]], [[McGinley Square]], [[India Square]], the [[Five Corners, Jersey City|Five Corners]] and parts of the [[Marion Section]].<ref>{{Cite book| publisher = Hagstrom Map Company, Inc| isbn = 978-0-88097-763-0| title = Hudson County New Jersey Street Map| year = 2008}}</ref> Many local, state, and federal agencies serving [[Hudson County]] maintain offices in the district.

==History==
[[File:Journal Square - Jersey City, NJ (55191652498).jpg|left|thumb|The Square was named for the ''[[Jersey Journal]]''.]]
[[Image:26JournalSquare.JPG|thumb|left|The [[26 Journal Square|Labor Bank Building]] at 26 Journal Square was the city's first skyscraper.]]

Prior to its development as a commercial district Journal Square was the site of many farmhouses and manors belonging to descendants of the original settlers of [[Bergen, New Netherland|Bergen]], the first chartered municipality in the state settled in 1660 and located just south at [[Bergen Square]]. In conjunction with the 1912 opening of the [[Hudson and Manhattan Railroad]] Summit Avenue station many of those properties were demolished to make way for modern buildings, including the still standing [[26 Journal Square|Labor Bank Building]] and the [[Public Service Railway|Public Service]] building. The [[Newkirk House]]<ref>[http://www.jclandmarks.com/newkirkhouse.shtml Newkirk House] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131004222428/http://jclandmarks.com/newkirkhouse.shtml |date=October 4, 2013 }}</ref> and [[Van Wagenen House]] remain, while the still-intact Sip Manor was moved to [[Westfield, New Jersey]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.njcu.edu/programs/jchistory/Pages/S_Pages/Sip_Manor_House.htm |title=Sip Manor House |publisher=Njcu.edu |access-date=November 1, 2008 |archive-date=December 29, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081229105231/http://www.njcu.edu/programs/jchistory/Pages/S_Pages/Sip_Manor_House.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> The square was created in 1923 when the city condemned and demolished the offices of the ''Jersey Journal'', thus creating a broad intersection with [[County Route 501 (New Jersey)|Hudson Boulevard]] which itself had been widened in 1908. The newspaper built new headquarters and the new square was named in its honor.<ref name="Grundy">{{cite book |last=Grundy
|first=J. Owen|title=The History of Jersey City (1609 - 1976)|year=1975|publisher=Walter E. Knight; Progress Printing Company
|location=Jersey City|chapter="I am the law.." |page=53}}</ref>

[[File:Blvd Bridge west arch jeh.jpg|thumb|left|Hudson County Boulevard Bridge]]

The bridge carrying the boulevard was designed by consulting engineer [[Abraham Burton Cohen]] and completed in 1926.<ref>Cohen, A. Burton. "Hudson County Boulevard Bridge Plaza." Purdue Engineering Review 21, No. 4 (May 1926): 3-6, 22.</ref> For most of the twentieth century Journal Square was the cultural entertainment center of [[Hudson County, New Jersey|Hudson County]],<ref name="canonmagazine.org">[https://web.archive.org/web/20160303180127/http://www.canonmagazine.org/.../friedman.html Eric M. Friedman, ''Journal Square and the Old Loew's Theatre: Grassroots Resistance in a City Center'', Canon Magazine, 2009]</ref> home to the [[movie palaces]] built in the 1920s: The State (1922, and since demolished),<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cinematreasures.org/theater/1630/|title=State Theater|work=cinematreasures.org|access-date=November 8, 2009|archive-date=July 28, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090728053913/http://cinematreasures.org/theater/1630/|url-status=live}}</ref> the [[Stanley Theater (Jersey City)|Stanley Theater]] (1928),<ref name="Stanely">[http://www.njcu.edu/.../Pages/.../Stanley_Theater.htm Stanely Theater]</ref> and the [[Loew's Jersey Theater]] (1929).<ref name="Loew's">[http://www.njcu.edu/Programs/.../L.../Loews_Jersey_Theater.htm Loew's Jersey]</ref> Karen Angel of ''[[The New York Daily News]]'' described Journal Square from the 1920s to the 1960s as a "crown jewel, a glowing commercial, entertainment and transportation hub of the city."<ref name="AngelKaren1">Angel, Karen. "Journal Squared: A Jersey City neighborhood's housing multiplies." ''[[The New York Daily News]]''. Friday November 13, 2009. [http://www.nydailynews.com/ny_local/your_neighborhood/2009/11/13/2009-11-13_journal_squared_a_.html 1] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091115143551/http://www.nydailynews.com/ny_local/your_neighborhood/2009/11/13/2009-11-13_journal_squared_a_.html |date=November 15, 2009 }}. Retrieved on November 13, 2009.</ref> The "[[Jersey Bounce]]", a hit song in the 1940s mentions Journal Square in its lyrics as the place where it got started. Two days before Election Day in 1960 [[John F. Kennedy]] made his last campaign speech at Journal Square, before returning to New England.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/ws/index.php?pid=25666|title=John F. Kennedy: Remarks of Senator John F. Kennedy, Journal Square, Jersey City, NJ|work=ucsb.edu|access-date=November 9, 2009|archive-date=November 22, 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081122082451/http://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/ws/index.php?pid=25666|url-status=live}}</ref> Hudson Boulevard was named [[County Route 501 (New Jersey)|Kennedy Boulevard]] soon after his assassination. The [[Tube Bar prank calls|Tube Bar]], so-called for the [[Downtown Hudson Tubes|Hudson Tubes]] (as the fore-runner of the PATH system was called) was made famous by Louis "Red" Deutsch getting prank calls there.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=J6TxcT7N9RgC&dq=tube%2Bbar%2Btapes&pg=PA110 Weird NJ Vol. 2 Tube Bar Interview] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240107152039/https://books.google.com/books?id=J6TxcT7N9RgC&dq=tube%2Bbar%2Btapes&pg=PA110#v=onepage&q=tube%2Bbar%2Btapes&f=false |date=January 7, 2024 }} Accessed May 12, 2009.</ref>

[[Image:Journal Sq dusk jeh.JPG|right|thumb|Journal Square at dusk]]
[[Image:India Square JC jeh.JPG|left|thumb|[[India Square]] on [[Newark Plank Road|Newark Avenue]]]]
The [[Journal Square Transportation Center]], opened between 1973 and 1975,<ref>{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20110612022048/http://www.panynj.gov/bus.../jstc-history.html|title=JSQ Trans Ctr history}}</ref> includes the [[Journal Square Transportation Center#Rapid transit|Journal Square PATH]] and bus station,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.panynj.gov/bus-terminals/journal-square-transportation-center.html|title=Journal Square Transportation Center - The Port Authority of NY & NJ|work=panynj.gov|access-date=October 8, 2009|archive-date=October 9, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091009005557/http://www.panynj.gov/bus-terminals/journal-square-transportation-center.html|url-status=live}}</ref> and is the headquarters of [[Port Authority Trans-Hudson|PATH]]. It is built on an elevated bridge structure above the [[Bergen Hill|Bergen Hill Cut]], an 1834 railroad [[Cut (earthmoving)|cut]] once used by [[Pennsylvania Railroad]] main line and [[Jersey City Branch]] and now by the [[Port Authority Trans-Hudson|PATH]] rapid transit system and an occasional freight train. In front of the station is a statue of [[Jackie Robinson]] who in 1946 crossed the [[baseball color line]] at [[Roosevelt Stadium]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.njcu.edu/programs/jchistory/Pages/R_Pages/Roosevelt_Stadium.htm |title=Roosevelt Stadium |access-date=May 22, 2009 |archive-date=December 25, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101225003447/http://www.njcu.edu/programs/jchistory/Pages/R_Pages/Roosevelt_Stadium.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>

A [[Statue of Christopher Columbus (Giacomoantonio)|statue of Christopher Columbus]], the work of Jersey City native Archimedes Giacomontonio, has been located on the square since 1950.<ref>[http://www.njcu.edu/.../Columbus_Christopher_Statue.htm Columbus Statue]</ref> The [[Stanley Theater (Jersey City)|Stanley]] and the [[Loew's Jersey Theater|Loew's]] have both been restored, the first now an Assembly Hall of [[Jehovah's Witnesses]],<ref name="Stanely"/> the latter used as a [[moviehouse]] and for other cultural events.<ref name="Loew's"/>

The campus of [[Hudson County Community College]] is a collection of buildings throughout the district around the square.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hccc.edu/|title=Hudson County Community College|work=hccc.edu|access-date=September 30, 2009|archive-date=September 8, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090908001605/http://hccc.edu/|url-status=live}}</ref> A few blocks to the south near [[McGinley Square]], are [[Saint Peter's University]], [[Hudson Catholic Regional High School]], and the [[Jersey City Armory]]. A concentration of [[Filipinos in New Jersey|Overseas Filipino]] and [[Indian American]]–operated shops<ref>can be found along [[Newark Plank Road|Newark Avenue]] and at [[India Square]].[http://www.thenewjournalsquare.com/html/press/indiasquare.htm "India Square"] accessed November 7, 2009 {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131015155533/http://www.thenewjournalsquare.com/html/press/indiasquare.htm |date=October 15, 2013 }}</ref> can be found along [[Newark Plank Road|Newark Avenue]] and near [[India Square]] to the north.

Northeast of Journal Square is [[Five Corners, Jersey City|Five Corners]], the ''[[county seat]]'' of [[Hudson County, New Jersey|Hudson County]].{{citation needed|date=June 2025}} The [[Hudson County Courthouse]], located at 583 Newark Avenue {{coord|40|43|55|N|74|3|25|W|name=Hudson County Courthouse}}, and the adjacent [[Hudson County Administration Building]], at 595 Newark Avenue, are home to the county's courts and a number of county agencies and departments. The Five Corners Branch of the Jersey City Public Library is sited on the intersection itself, while [[William L. Dickinson High School]] is located nearby at 2 [[Palisade Avenue (Hudson Palisades)|Palisade Avenue]].

==High-rise development==
{{update|section|date=December 2025}}
[[File:Journal Square Jersey City November 2021 004.jpg|thumb|right|Aerial view looking northwest to Journal Square]]
Many of the buildings in Journal Square include housing stock (such as [[brownstone]]s, pre-war apartment buildings, and Frame houses), [[convenience store]]s, bodegas, and downscale franchises, that [[Jerremiah Healy]], [[Mayor of Jersey City]], has referred to as "ugly old eyesores."<ref name="AngelKaren1"/> The redevelopment of Journal Square has attracted the interest of urban planners, architects, sociologists, and others, many who view its historical, current, and future use as an important indicator of the contemporary understanding of how cities function.<ref name="canonmagazine.org"/><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.jerseycitymuseum.org/exhib_dtl.cfm?exhibid=64 |title=JC Museum: (Re)Centering: New Visions for Journal Square |access-date=November 9, 2009 |archive-date=December 31, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151231171434/http://www.jerseycitymuseum.org/exhib_dtl.cfm?exhibid=64 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>[http://www.thenewjournalsquare.com/.../JS_Redevelopment_Plans.html JSQ Redevelopment Plans]{{dead link|date=December 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://thejcra.org/jcra_files/File/development_projects/journal_square/Redevelopment_Plan_submitted_to_City_Council_after_caucuspdf.pdf |title=Redevelop Journal Square City Center |access-date=November 18, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110728094658/http://thejcra.org/jcra_files/File/development_projects/journal_square/Redevelopment_Plan_submitted_to_City_Council_after_caucuspdf.pdf |archive-date=July 28, 2011 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite report |title=Journal Square 2060 |publisher=Jersey City Planning Department |url=https://www.scribd.com/doc/34274347/Draft-Journal-Square-2060-Redevelopment-Pla |access-date=May 15, 2011 |archive-date=January 7, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240107152041/https://www.scribd.com/document/34274347/Draft-Journal-Square-2060-Redevelopment-Plan |url-status=live }}</ref>

A proposed development by [[Kushner Real Estate Group]] and National Real Estate Advisors, [[Journal Squared]], was announced as a 2.3 million square foot, 3-tower residential complex. The first phase, a 53-story tower, opened in early 2017.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.yimbynews.com/2017/03/ribbon-cut-for-first-tower-of-journal-squared-in-jersey-city.html|title=Ribbon Cut for First Tower of Journal Squared in Jersey City – New York YIMBY|website=www.yimbynews.com|language=en-US|access-date=March 21, 2017|archive-date=March 22, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170322015513/http://www.yimbynews.com/2017/03/ribbon-cut-for-first-tower-of-journal-squared-in-jersey-city.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> The final phase was completed in 2025.<ref>{{cite web | last=Eberhardt | first=Ellen | title=Three connected white-clad skyscrapers completed in New Jersey | publisher=Dezeen | date=2025-04-16 | url=https://www.dezeen.com/2025/04/16/three-skyscraper-journal-squared-development-new-jersey/ | access-date=2026-10-15}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last=Walsh | first=Niall Patrick | title=HWKN completes final tower of Journal Squared in New Jersey | website=Archinect | url=https://archinect.com/news/article/150474488/hwkn-completes-final-tower-of-journal-squared-in-new-jersey | access-date=2026-10-15}}</ref> It sits directly adjacent to the Journal Square PATH station as a continuation of the dense transit-oriented development that has arisen further to the east in Jersey City. The towers were designed by Hollwich Kushner and Handel Architects.

In October 2011, MEPT purchased [[Newport Tower (Jersey City)|Newport Tower]] on the Hudson waterfront for $377 million, a record price for an office real estate transaction in the state.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Edward |first=Daniel |url=http://www.commercialobserver.com/2011/10/new-jerseys-biggest-tower-sale-ever/ |title=New Jersey's Biggest Tower Sale… Ever! |publisher=Commercial Observer |date=October 19, 2011 |access-date=April 24, 2014 |archive-date=April 24, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140424234306/http://commercialobserver.com/2011/10/new-jerseys-biggest-tower-sale-ever/ |url-status=live }}</ref> A further extension to 2013 requested by MEPTA was not granted by the Jersey City Redevelopment Agency.<ref>{{Cite news |last=McDonald |first=Terrence T. |title=Developer Threatens to Sue Jersey City Agency over Comments Made to The Jersey Journal |newspaper=The Jersey Journal |date=April 26, 2014 |url=http://www.nj.com/hudson/index.ssf/2012/04/journal_square_developer_threa.html |access-date=December 11, 2014 |archive-date=December 20, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141220054340/http://www.nj.com/hudson/index.ssf/2012/04/journal_square_developer_threa.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Jersey City is one of nine municipalities in New Jersey designated as eligible for Urban Transit Hub Tax Credits by the state's [[New Jersey Economic Development Authority|Economic Development Authority]].<ref>[https://www.njeda.com/urban-transit-hub-tax-credit-program/ Urban Transit Hub Tax Credit Program] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230424172720/https://www.njeda.com/urban-transit-hub-tax-credit-program/ |date=April 24, 2023 }}, [[New Jersey Economic Development Authority]]. Accessed April 24, 2023. "Urban Transit Hubs are located within ½ mile of New Jersey Transit, PATH, PATCO, or light rail stations in Camden (expanded to one mile), East Orange, Elizabeth, Hoboken, Jersey City, Newark, New Brunswick, Paterson, and Trenton."</ref> Developers who invest a minimum of $50 million within {{Convert|0.5|mi}} of a train station are eligible for pro-rated [[tax credit]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Urban Transit Hub Tax Credits |work=Financing Programs |publisher=New Jersey Economic Development Authority |url=http://www.njeda.com/web/Aspx_pg/Templates/Npic_Text.aspx?Doc_Id=888&menuid=1295&topid=718&levelid=6&midid=1175 |access-date=December 28, 2013 |archive-date=April 14, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120414152339/http://www.njeda.com/web/Aspx_pg/Templates/Npic_Text.aspx?Doc_Id=888&menuid=1295&topid=718&levelid=6&midid=1175 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=NEW JERSEY ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY Urban Transit Hub Tax Credit Program Approved Projects |work=Urban Transit Hub Tax Credits |publisher=New Jersey Economic Development Authority |date=December 3, 2013 |url=http://www.njeda.com/web/pdf/HUB_Activity.pdf |access-date=December 28, 2013 |archive-date=December 30, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131230233614/http://www.njeda.com/web/pdf/HUB_Activity.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In December 2012 the ''[[Jersey Journal]]'' sold its building and relocated to Harmon Plaza in nearby [[Secaucus]];<ref name=autogenerated1>{{cite news |last=McDonald |first=Terrence T. |title=The Jersey Journal finalizing sale of its Journal Square offices in Jersey City |newspaper=The Jersey Journal |date=December 5, 2012 |url=http://www.nj.com/hudson/index.ssf/2012/12/the_jersey_journal_finalizing.html |access-date=December 11, 2014 |archive-date=December 20, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141220055906/http://www.nj.com/hudson/index.ssf/2012/12/the_jersey_journal_finalizing.html |url-status=live }}</ref> however, a large sign with the paper's name was still in place atop the building in the square as of June 2015.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.google.com/maps/@40.7313846,-74.064117,3a,75y,182.08h,90.38t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sueCpC5n1MjeAo-xv_El4Cw!2e0!7i13312!8i6656!6m1!1e1 |title=Google Street View shot, dated June 2015, of Journal Square, Jersey City, with "Jersey Journal" signage atop a building (near the center of the photo) |access-date=January 2, 2016 |archive-date=February 5, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160205051557/https://www.google.com/maps/@40.7313846,-74.064117,3a,75y,182.08h,90.38t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sueCpC5n1MjeAo-xv_El4Cw!2e0!7i13312!8i6656!6m1!1e1 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2024, the Jersey City Council adopted a [[zoning]] ordinance for Journal Square, requiring that new residential projects with over 30 apartments set aside either 10% or 15% as [[affordable housing]], based on that census tract's income.<ref>{{cite web | last=Milone | first=Andy | title=Council Adopts Controversial Journal Square Affordable Housing Ordinance | website=Jersey City Times | date=2024-08-16 | url=https://jcitytimes.com/council-adopts-controversial-journal-square-affordable-housing-ordinance/ | access-date=2026-10-15}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=August 15, 2024 |title=Jersey City council adopts limited affordable housing plan for Journal Square, with reservations |url=https://www.nj.com/hudson/2024/08/jersey-city-council-adopts-boggianos-limited-affordable-housing-plan-for-journal-square-with-reservations.html |access-date=2026-10-15 |work=nj |language=en}}</ref> In the 2020s, other mixed-use projects were completed or planned throughout the district.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nj.com/hudson/2022/02/the-journal-square-transformation-is-looking-up-way-up.html|title=The Journal Square transformation is looking up -- way up|date=February 10, 2022|access-date=February 15, 2022|archive-date=February 15, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220215182137/https://www.nj.com/hudson/2022/02/the-journal-square-transformation-is-looking-up-way-up.html|url-status=live}}</ref> 2859-2873 John F. Kennedy Boulevard, a 55-story tower near the [[Loew's Jersey Theatre]], was approved in April 2026,<ref>{{cite web | last=Fry | first=Chris | title=Jersey City Approves 55-Story Tower with Whole Foods Market | website=Jersey Digs | date=2026-04-28 | url=https://jerseydigs.com/2859-2873-kennedy-blvd-jersey-city-approved/ | access-date=2026-10-15}}</ref> and 547-555 Summit Avenue, a 47-story twin-tower development, was approved that September.<ref>{{cite web | title=First Phase of Jersey City Multifamily Secures $310M Financing | website=Connect CRE | date=2026-09-27 | url=https://www.connectcre.com/stories/first-phase-of-jersey-city-multifamily-secures-310m-financing/ | access-date=2026-10-15}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Construction Awaits For 1,517-Unit Skyscraper at 547-555 Summit Avenue In Journal Square, Jersey City | website=New York YIMBY | date=2026-09-28 | url=https://newyorkyimby.com/2026/09/construction-awaits-for-1517-unit-skyscraper-at-547-555-summit-avenue-in-journal-square-jersey-city.html | access-date=2026-10-15}}</ref>
